questions.q: What is the correct planning order this lesson gives for a SQL Server migration to Azure?
options: Pick a target first, then define success criteria, then inventory what exists
Define success criteria first, then pick a target, then inventory afterward
Inventory what exists, then define success criteria, then pick a target
Skip inventory entirely and migrate directly to whichever target is cheapest
questions.explain: The lesson insists on this exact order: you cannot plan around a database you haven't measured, and you cannot evaluate a target without knowing what success requires.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call picking a target first "the most common planning mistake"?
options: Teams often choose the cheapest target, then discover a feature dependency mid-migration and have to re-plan
Because targets can never be changed once chosen, even before migration starts
Because Managed Instance is technically incapable of being migrated to
Because Azure SQL Database is always the correct target regardless of dependencies
questions.explain: This is the exact scenario the lesson describes as the common failure mode of skipping inventory and success criteria.

questions.q: What should a migration inventory capture, per this lesson?
options: Only the version number of SQL Server currently installed
Every instance, every database, its size, and what depends on it — linked servers, cross-database queries, SSIS packages, connection strings
Only the total dollar cost of the current on-prem hardware
Only the names of the DBAs currently responsible for each server
questions.explain: The inventory needs to be complete enough to reveal dependencies that could block or complicate a chosen target.

questions.q: What should "success criteria" for a migration look like, according to this lesson?
options: Concrete written numbers — a maximum downtime window, a performance floor, a cost ceiling — defined before evaluating any target
A criteria set only the cloud vendor is allowed to define
A vague statement that the migration should "go well"
Whatever performance the migration happens to produce, judged after the fact
questions.explain: Writing these down as concrete numbers before picking a target prevents "success" from being redefined after the fact.

questions.q: What T-SQL skill does this lesson say the inventory step reuses, rather than requiring new tools?
options: System-catalog queries against views like sys.databases, the same kind of query already learned in T-SQL Development
Creating a new Elastic Job target group
Configuring a private endpoint and VNet
Writing a brand-new PowerShell module from scratch
questions.explain: The lesson's example query against sys.databases is the same catalog-query skill redirected toward migration inventory.
